3. The respondent No. 1 is the husband of the petitioner and the father of the detenu child. Respondent Nos. 2 and 3 are the nephews of the respondent No. 1 and respondent No. 4 is the paternal grand mother of the detenu child. The petitioner spent her early adult life along with the aforesaid children in England. Soon after the marriage respondent No. 1 disclosed to his wife, the petitioner, that he was not a British citizen and being instructed by him she applied to the immigration authorities for leave for him to remain in Britain by reason of the marriage. At that time respondent No. 1 owned 1/3 (one third) share of a restaurant and also worked as a waiter in that restaurant. In pursuance of the application the respondent No. 1 received his British residency. Soon after he obtained British residency the relationship between the petitioner and the respondent No. 1 began to deteriorate. Firstly, the petitioner was subjected to random verbal abuse and mental cruelty and the respondent No. 1 found fault with her in every action, taunted her and humiliated her in private and also in public. Within a few months the respondent No. 1 began physical assaults. The petitioner was on various occasions slapped and punched on her back, on the stomach, thrown against the wall, tables and on door, and even on occasion forced to have sexual relations with the respondent No. 1 following threats of further physical violence. All such assaults frequently followed bouts of drinking by the respondent No. 1. In spite of all these the petitioner tried her utmost to protect the children from the impact of his such violence. The petitioner's marital life was lived in a cycle of abuse, assaults by the respondent No. 1 and the petitioner continued to silently suffer such brutal assaults in the desperate hope that the abuse would cease and in an attempt to somehow keep the marriage tie. The petitioner did not even inform her father of the abuse because her father arranged the marriage. In November, 1993 the respondent No. 1 brought the petitioner and their four children to Bangladesh on the clear understanding to the petitioner that they were coming on a short visit. Respondent No. 1 took the passports of the petitioner and the four children soon after their arrival at Zia International Airport, Dhaka and till to-day did not return the same. In 19 months thereafter respondent No. 1 returned to England on several occasions, spending only a few months with the petitioner and the children. The respondent No. 1 hired a house at Uttara and insisted for admitting two of the children in Sunrise School at Uttara on the plea that they will improve Bangla before returning to England. The petitioner pleaded to respondent No. 1 to return with the children to their home in England but she was subjected to further physical abuse. On 8-5-95 in the morning the respondent No. 1 aided by the respondent Nos. 2 and 3 including his other relatives from his paternal village deceitfully and illegally removed all the four children from the custody of the petitioner. The petitioner later came to know that the respondent No. 1 had sent for the petitioner's father. The detenu children were removed from the house by the respondent Nos. 2 and 3 on the instructions of the respondent No. 1 and were taken to the paternal home of the respondent No.1 where they have remained since. Thereafter the petitioner received a copy of notice dated 10-7-95 of divorce dated 9-7-95 issued by the respondent No. 1 in pursuance of section 7 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, 1961. The petitioner and her father were then ordered to leave the house also. The petitioner came to learn that the children are neglected by the respondent No. 1 who was considering of another marriage shortly. The petitioner in such circumstances through her family members tried to recover the children from the illegal custody of respondent No. 1 but respondent No. 1 not only refused to return the children but also threatened to kill her if she makes any attempt to recover the detenu children. The petitioner being a British citizen in a desperate attempt to recover the detenu children then travelled to England to seek legal assistance and being advised she filed a suit for recovery of the detenu children in the High Court of Justice (Family Division). The High Court of Justice was pleased to pass an order on 12-7-95 directing that the detenu children be made wards of the Court and that they be returned by the respondent No.1 to the jurisdiction of the court. The Court of Justice by an order dated 14-7-95 directed that the respondent No. 1 be forbidden from seeking to prevent or delay the petitioner from bringing the detenu children to the jurisdiction of the Court with a further direction that the respondent No.1 to forthwith hand over the detenu children to the physical care of the petitioner and the children shall remain in the interim care and control of the petitioner until further order. The copies of the orders are annexed as Annexures-B and E to this petition. It is further alleged that the detenu children have been illegally and deceitfully removed from the lawful custody of the petitioner mother. Furthermore, the petitioner is entitled to recover the custody of the detenu children pursuant to the aforementioned orders of the High Court of Justice (Family Division), England whereby legal custody of the detenu children vests in the petitioner in the interest and welfare of the children one of which, being a breastfeeding infant. The petitioner being the mother of the detenu children having genuine love and affection for the children has devoted her entire life for their upbringing. The petitioner served a demand justice notice through her lawyer asking the respondents to return back the children but there was no response, hence these petitions under Article 102 (2)(b)(i) of the Constitution in the nature of Habeas Corpus. 

 4. The petitions are resisted by the respondents by filing four separate affidavits-in opposition supplementary affidavit-in-opposition exactly on the same contention denying all material allegations made in the petitions. In the affidavit-in-oppositions it is stated by the respondent No. 1 that he is a citizen of Bangladesh and on 27-4-76 went to London and had been serving there at different places. While in service in London being acquainted with the father of the petitioner through his maternal uncle and on being proposed by the father of the petitioner he was married to his daughter Sharon Laily Begum. During their marriage life 2 daughters and 2 sons were born. Last one born on 9-8-93 aged about 22 months. During that time respondent No. 1 had been running the restaurant business. Seeing the life style of the teen-aged children in London, specially their free mixing immoral social life, spending time at night clubs, the petitioner, in consideration of the future welfare of the minors proposed to respondent No.1 to take her and their children to Bangladesh to rear up them in Bangladeshi culture and education Accordingly on their mutual understanding respondent No. 1 brought all of them to Bangladesh on 12-11-93 and hired House No. 24, Road No. 16, Sector No. 3 at Uttara Model Town and got two elder children admitted in Sun Rise Pre-Cadet School and thereafter transferred to an International School, Dhanmondi, Dhaka. It is further stated therein that the respondent No. 1 keeping his wife and minor children in Bangladesh left for London to his place of business and used to keep regular contact with the petitioner over telephone. For comfort of the petitioner she was given a Pajero Jeep, 3/4 servants and a driver and to look after them one A. Rahim, a nephew of the respondent No.1, also was kept in the house and thereby spent huge amount of money more than 10 (ten) lakh since 1993 to June 1995. The respondent No.1 came back again to Bangladesh in the year 1994 during the Eid holidays and stayed upto July, 1994. During that time one of his brothers Mr. Mozahar who had been serving in America came to Bangladesh and married one Hazera Begum and keeping her with the petitioner left for America. Respondent No. 1 again came back to Bangladesh in September, 1994 and during his stay in Bangladesh observing some changes in the living style of the petitioner the father of the petitioner was called at the house at Uttara and disclosed the same to him. At this the petitioner became very much annoyed with the respondent No. 1 but considering the welfare of his children tried to rectify her and after prolonged attempt the petitioner assured that she will not repeat the same and on believing the same in good faith he left for London again. He regularly kept contact with the petitioner and other members of the family over telephone but occasionally found some other person in male voice used to receive the telephone and put it down without answering anything and most of the time the petitioner used to be out of the house. This created suspicion in the mind of the respondent No. 1 and he sent his brother from America to Dhaka who from his wife, maid servant Fatema and driver came to know that the petitioner is leading an immoral life living with different male persons spending nights outside and is not taking any care of the children and informed the respondent No. 1. On receipt of such information respondent No. 1 rushed to Bangladesh on 19-1-95 and after ascertaining the allegations against his wife found all to be correct which was also confirmed by the said servant, driver and the brother's wife in the house informing further that the petitioner had been illegally keeping immoral connection with one Masud and had been living with him at home and outside. It was reported that the petitioner totally neglected her children and even would not give any care to the breast sucking baby and threatened the maid servant Fatema not to disclose about her activities to anybody and the nephew of the respondent No.1 would most of the time be sent out of the house on various pretexts and sometimes he was sent to their village home. Respondent No. 1 made attempts to rectify his wife and the petitioner admitting all her immoral activities, apologised and assured again that she will forget her past and will be at home with the children and shall not keep contact with any boy friend including Masud. On such assurance the respondent No. 1 returned to London to run his business in February, 1995. After his departure the petitioner resorted to her immoral activities again totally giving up looking after her children rather started showing hatred towards them. Hearing all these the respondent No. 1 again came to Bangladesh on 28-4-95 and on his arrival did not find the petitioner at home. He discovered a diary of the petitioner where she in her own hand had written all her activities including future plans regarding her intention to marry Masud. The photo copy of the diary is marked as Annexure-1 to the affidavit-in-oppositions. On that date at 10-00 PM the petitioner returned home and seeing the respondent No. 1 became furious and started abusing him with filthy words and at one stage she threatened the respondent No. 1 not to interfere in her way of life otherwise she will kill him. Having no other alternative respondent No. 1 informed his father-in-law who immediately came to the house at Uttara. It was also transpired to the respondent No. 1 that by this time the petitioner removed about Taka. 2(two) lakh in cash including gold ornaments and her passport and this gave rise to the mind of the respondent No.1 that the petitioner was thus so desperate she may do any, harm to him as well as her children. For his safety and the children he lodged a General Diary with Uttara Police Station on 6-5-95 being GD Entry No. 283. Then on 9-5-95 the respondent No. 1 divorced the petitioner and lodged another General Diary with Uttara Police Station being GD Entry No. 451 seeking protection of police. The respondent No. 1 also made another General Diary on 10-5-95 being GD Entry No. 481 stating that the petitioner was with her father. On 10-5-95 after the petitioner was divorced by respondent No. 1 her father took her to his custody with written acknowledgement signing on a non-judicial stamp and also by filing a GD Entry being No. 491 on 10-5-95. It is further stated that after the divorce the petitioner went to her father's house at her own will and that for the welfare of the children they were brought to Bangladesh with the petitioner but the petitioner totally disregarded her responsibility in the absence of respondent No. 1 which has seriously affected the welfare of the minor children. It is stated that the petitioner after her divorce allowed the children to be with the father and in her General Diary Annexure-3(a) she claimed the passport only not the children which clearly proves that the children were not in any way unlawfully detained by respondent No. 1 and the children were under the care of their grand-mother respondent no. 4 assisted by the respondent No. 1 who are competent to look after the welfare of the minors. It is further stated that the respondent No.1 has already filed an application under section 25(i) of the Guardians and Wards Act read with section 5 of the Muslim Family Court Ordinance before the Family Court on 30-7-95 -being Family Suit No. 145 of 1995 and summons were served upon the petitioner and the case is now pending where the dispute between the parties shall be decided finally and the instant Writ Petitions are not maintainable. 

 6. Dr. Kamal Hossain, the learned Counsel for the petitioner, submits that all the detenu children have been illegally and deceitfully removed from the lawful custody of the petitioner and are being illegally detained by the respondents and the respondents arc obliged under the law to return the detenu children to the lawful custody of the petitioner-mother. He submits that according to the established principles of law it is for the interest and welfare of the children to be in the custody of the mother-petitioner, particularly in view of the respondent No.1's being prone to recurrent violence and abuse. He also submits that the petitioner is entitled to the custody of the detenu children being their mother having genuine love and affection for the children and having devoted her entire adult life for their upbringing. He next contends that the detention of the infant child is otherwise unwarranted in law and on the facts and has been made without lawful authority and in total disregard of the interest and welfare of the detenu children. He also submits that the detenu children being illegally detained the petitioner is entitled to recover their custody pursuant to the orders of the High Court of Justice (Family Division) whereby legal custody of the detenu children vests in the petitioner. He lastly, submits that the provision of Muslim Personal Law of the parties is applicable in these cases and refers to section 352 of the Mohammedan Law. 

 7. Mr. Serajul Huq, the learned Advocate for the respondents, frankly concedes that in view of the provision of law provided in this regard the petitioner may have the custody of the children but in such cases the welfare of the children is to be considered as prime. He submits that considering all aspects in the matter particularly regarding immoral leading of life by the petitioner, the children should not be given to her custody considering their welfare and interest. He submits that the respondent No. 1 has already filed a case in the Family Court for guardianship where all matters in dispute shall be decided finally. In such circumstances the writ petitions are not maintainable. 

 9. Admittedly out of the 4(four) minor children 3 (three) of them namely; Jasmin Akthar Jalil (female), Sharlean Akthar Jalil (female) and Shah Alam Jalil (male) were born on 8-9-88, 24-4-91 and 9-8-93 respectively. Amongst them two are female child and the male child namely, Shah Alam Jalil, is of about 22 months of age only. In view of the provision of Muslim Personal Law of the parties as provided under section 352 of the Mohammedan Law the mother- petitioner is entitled to the custody of the aforesaid 3 minor children. By giving those 3 children to the custody of the mother-petitioner they are deemed to set them at liberty from unlawful custody of the respondents in exercise of the court's power under writ jurisdiction. 

 11. The question of maintainability of these writ petitions in the nature of Habeas Corpus for the custody of the minor children raised by Mr. Serajul Huq, the learned Advocate for the respondents, is of no substance. Our answer is in the affirmative. In the case of Ayesha Khanam and others vs. Major Sabbir Ahmed and others, reported in 46 DLR 399 a Division Bench of this Court relying on the decisions reported in AIR 1960 (SC) 93, AIR 1979 (All) 25 and AIR 1984 (SC) 1224, held that: 

 Article 102(2)(b) of the Constitution is very wide in nature as it provided that any person and not only aggrieved person as in mandamus or certiorari or quo warranto can take to the notice of the court that somebody is illegally detained by any person and pray for a declaration that the person is so detained illegally and without lawful authority and the court shall, after being so satisfied, direct the person to be set at liberty at once." 

 "A petition in this nature of habeas corpus for the custody of a minor would also be equally competent without sending the petitioner to exhaust his or her remedy before the Family Court or under the Guardians and Wards Act or other criminal Court which is neither expedient nor an equally efficacious remedy in a situation like this and, in fact, a habeas corpus petition would give her the most speedy and efficacious remedy."
